intel_2026.whatItMeans: This is your classic restaurant code — any place that serves food in a permanent building. Sit-down restaurants, warungs with concrete walls, fast food joints, food courts inside malls, even hotel restaurants. If people walk in, sit down, and eat food you cooked in a fixed building, this is the code.
intel_2026.whatYouNeed:
**Micro scale** (smallest operations): Medium-Low risk. You get your NIB + Standard Certificate automatically — no waiting. You'll need a Hygiene Sanitation Label (HSP) and must submit periodic activity reports.

**Small / Medium / Large scale**: Medium-High risk. NIB + Standard Certificate issued within **14 working days**. You'll need a Self-Assessment of Standard Readiness, a certified standard from an LSPr (certification body), and a Hygiene Sanitation Feasibility Certificate (SLHS).

**PMA (foreign investment):** Fully open — 100% foreign ownership allowed.
intel_2026.whatChanged: Correction (2026-07-18): this code's merge list was fixed. The 2025 code 56101 (permanent-building restaurants) absorbs KBLI 2020 code 56102 (Rumah/Warung Makan — home-style eateries) and KBLI 2020 code 56109 (other fixed-building food) — that's it. If you previously operated under KBLI 2020 code 56103 (food stalls/tents) or 56104 (self-service/cafeteria restaurants), those are non-permanent-structure food activities and now fall under KBLI 2025 code 56102 ('Aktivitas Penyediaan Makanan di Bangunan Tidak Tetap'), not this code — check that page instead.
intel_2026.baliContext: This is the single most common business code for foreigners in Bali. Seminyak, Canggu, and Ubud are saturated — the competition is fierce and landlords know it. Sanur and Uluwatu still have room. Keep in mind: Bali's health department (Dinas Kesehatan) does actual inspections for your SLHS, and they check kitchen hygiene, water quality, and food storage. Budget 2-4 weeks for the inspection alone. Also, most Bali restaurants need a separate liquor license if they serve alcohol — 56101 alone doesn't cover that.

editorial.headline: A Fixed-Premises Food Business, Fully Foreign-Open Nationally
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 56101 covers food-service operations from permanent premises, with a clear national opening to foreign investment and no Bali moratorium block at Large scale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56101 is the framework for providing food to customers from a fixed, permanent building: a place that is not designed to be dismantled, moved or operated as a travelling venue. It encompasses table service where dishes are cooked to order, as well as counter and buffet formats where customers take, or are served, food already on display. Meals may be eaten on the premises, taken away, or delivered to the customer’s home. In practical terms, this is the home of restaurants, eating houses, canteens and cafeterias, fast-food restaurants, and take-away restaurants.

Its reach is deliberately broader than the classic street-facing dining room. A separately operated restaurant inside a hotel belongs here when it is not part of the hotel business itself. The same separate-unit principle applies to restaurants in transport facilities and aboard transport, as well as a take-away restaurant inside a supermarket. Catering restaurants and ice-cream or yoghurt outlets are also within the stated scope. The constant is not the menu or service style; it is an independently operated food-service business based in a fixed setting.

Businesses may register at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. The activity is TERBUKA to foreign investment nationally, subject to a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That is a straightforward national position: a foreign investor can hold the entire permitted stake, rather than needing to infer a lower limit from the nature of a food business or from the way it serves customers.

Bali requires a more precise reading, but not a more pessimistic one. The province’s permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. This activity is not blocked by that rule: at Besar scale, its OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, and the Bali assessment is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK. For a foreign founder considering a fixed-premises food operation in Bali, the record therefore does not present a Bali moratorium prohibition. The national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling remains the relevant ownership position, while the Bali result is expressly one of no moratorium block at the stated risk profile.

editorial.headline: Fermented Fish Processing, With a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 10215 covers fermented fish preservation and fish-based condiments, open nationally to all business scales and not blocked for PMA in Bali under the record.
editorial.body:
KBLI 10215 is a focused food-processing activity: the treatment and preservation of finfish through fermentation. The record names familiar product forms rather than abstract industrial language: fermented fish such as ikan peda and ikan kayu, plus fish sauce and fish terasi. In plain English, this is the category for businesses that turn fish into preserved, fermented products where time, salt, process control, and handling transform the raw material into a stable food ingredient or finished condiment.

That makes the activity broader than one product line but still tightly bounded. It is not a general seafood-trading category and not a catch-all for every marine product. Its centre of gravity is processing and preservation, specifically by fermentation, and specifically for finfish and fish-derived fermented outputs named in the scope. A founder choosing this activity should read the scope as a production classification: the business is making or preserving these fish-based fermented goods, not merely branding them, distributing them, or operating a restaurant that happens to serve them.

The registration picture is unusually clean in the slim record. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales, so the classification is not limited to one enterprise size. Nationally, its PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. That means the record presents KBLI 10215 as nationally open to foreign ownership up to the full stated ceiling. There is no lower percentage in the record, and there is no separate Bali ownership cap to add on top of it.

The Bali reading is also direct. The record marks the Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK and says l4_bali_blocked is false. The moratorium rule in the record says Bali blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently; this activity is not blocked under that rule because the record’s Bali reason states: “OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium.” So the honest national-vs-Bali picture is not a hidden contradiction. Nationally, it is open; in Bali, the record does not mark it as blocked by the PMA moratorium. For this code, the decisive point is restraint: use the national 100% ceiling, use the recorded Bali status, and do not invent a Bali-side percentage or extra local condition that the record does not contain.

**TRIPLE-LOCKED IN BALI (as of Feb 2026):** This code is blocked three ways:
- **Lock 1:** 0% PMA — foreigners cannot own it, period
- **Lock 2:** Governor has asked BKPM to close OSS for all low-risk PMA in Bali
- **Lock 3:** Instruksi Gubernur No. 6/2025 — MORATORIUM on all new Toko Modern Berjejaring (chain modern store) permits across Bali, both PBG and business licenses

---

**The moratorium explained:** The Governor's response to the explosive growth of Alfamart and Indomaret, which has devastated traditional warung and pasar. Addressed to all 9 Bupati/Walikota and DPMPTSP heads across Bali. Remains in effect until a provincial Perda on chain store control is enacted — which could take **years**.

- **Nominee structure** — the single most dangerous legal move a foreigner can make in Indonesia. Asset seizure, deportation, and criminal charges are real outcomes
- **Confusing 47111 with 47192** — 47111 is self-service food retail (0% PMA), 47192 is non-food retail (100% PMA open). The difference: whether food/beverages dominate your inventory

editorial.headline: Self-Service Food Retail: National Limits and Bali’s Closed Door
editorial.standfirst: This code covers self-service retail led by food, beverages or tobacco, yet its national foreign-ownership ceiling is 0% and Bali expressly closes it to PMA.
editorial.body:
This activity is the self-service retailing of a broad mix of everyday goods in which food ingredients, prepared food, beverages or tobacco remain the dominant offer. Prices are set in advance; customers select items themselves and pay at a cashier. The format may also sell selected non-food items—household furnishings, children’s toys, medicines, medical devices and clothing—but these do not alter the central character of the business: food, beverages or tobacco lead the assortment. Hypermarkets and supermarkets are expressly within its scope.

The code is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That matters because scale does not dilute the operating identity. Whether the enterprise is small or large, it remains a self-service retailer whose principal merchandise is food, beverages or tobacco, with any permitted non-food range remaining secondary to that retail core.

Nationally, the PMA position is limited, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 0%. In practical terms, the record does not present this as a route for foreign equity participation. The applicable national reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. A registration decision should therefore begin with the actual retail model—self-service checkout, predetermined prices and a food-, beverage- or tobacco-led range—rather than with the presence of ancillary household or consumer goods on the shelves.

Bali is more direct still. The provincial status is closed, and the stated reason is that minimarkets and supermarkets are reserved for Indonesian citizens and closed to PMA. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today through PMA. Bali also maintains an island-wide, permanent block on PMA for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities; the record identifies that provincial rule separately. The essential conclusion is not a matter of branding or store size: this self-service retail activity is nationally limited to a 0% foreign-ownership ceiling and expressly closed to PMA in Bali.

editorial.headline: Scheduled Ferries Across Provinces, With a Clear Bali Position
editorial.standfirst: This is the large-scale, route-bound public ferry business moving passengers between Indonesian provinces — foreign ownership in it is capped at 49%.
editorial.body:
Interprovincial public ferry passenger transport is the business of carrying passengers from one province to another on ferries operating on established routes. The route-bound character matters: this is public passenger movement organised through a ferry service, rather than an incidental voyage or a loosely defined maritime activity. Its commercial identity is shaped by regular interprovincial connection and the practical work of moving people across provincial boundaries by ferry.

The record opens this activity at the **Besar** scale. That places the code in a large-business setting: an operator registering under it is entering the public ferry transport field at that stated scale, with the focus on passenger carriage across provinces and on services tied to designated routes. The classification does not broaden into a general account of every kind of water transport; its centre of gravity is specific, public, scheduled ferry travel between provinces.

Foreign ownership here is capped at 49%. Interprovincial public passenger ferry transport is listed in Perpres 49/2021, Lampiran III — the annex of business fields carrying specific requirements — at entry #18, and that entry limits foreign shareholding to 49%. A PT PMA can hold up to that 49% and no more; the rest of the shares cannot be in foreign hands. The record carries the ceiling and nothing beyond it: no named partner, no minimum stake for any single shareholder, and no recorded route for exceeding the cap. The ceiling is national — registering the company somewhere other than Bali does not change it.

Bali does not add a second obstacle. The island-wide moratorium suspends new PMA registration only for activities assessed at low or medium-low risk. This one is recorded at medium-high risk, so the moratorium does not reach it and the company can be registered here. Bali states no percentage of its own and no local partnership requirement; what limits the foreign side is the 49% ceiling, in Bali exactly as anywhere else in Indonesia.
editorial.pullQuote: For large-scale interprovincial ferry transport, Bali's moratorium is not the constraint — the 49% ceiling on foreign shareholding is.

editorial.headline: Residential Development in Indonesia: Open Nationally, Watched Closely in Bali
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 68111 covers the business of developing, trading, leasing and operating residential property, from homes and flats to apartments and projects built for sale.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68111 is the activity code for residential building and land development. Its scope reaches beyond construction in the narrow sense: it includes the purchase and sale of residential buildings, including apartment buildings and homes; the development of houses, flats and apartments, furnished or unfurnished, for more permanent or year-round use; residential mobile-home sites intended as a main home; and residential building projects developed for sale. It also encompasses the purchase, sale, leasing and operation of housing that is either owned or rented, including residential or mixed-residential housing development.

This is therefore a code for the commercial life of housing as well as its creation. A business registered under it may be concerned with bringing a residential project to market, holding and operating housing, or arranging the ownership and rental activity surrounding it. The classification is open to Micro, Small, Medium and Large enterprises, placing it across the full stated range of business scales rather than reserving the activity for a particular size of operator.

At the national level, the foreign-investment position is direct: the activity is **open** to PMA, with a maximum foreign ownership of **100%**. The cited basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. In practical editorial terms, the national record does not present a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity.
